intro: Five long reads: what a child's death reveals about China's fast-track gene-therapy trials, the AI fortunes now paying for research on AI, why science's famous lucky accidents mostly weren't, the cracks a 20-year survey has found in cosmology's standard model, and the case that horses, not grain, made the first states.

stories.headline: A child's death and China's fast-track trials
stories.dek: Jane Qiu argues that a four-year-old's death after experimental gene editing in Shanghai exposes a system built to reward speed and hype, and that new rules alone will not fix it.
body: In March 2023 a four-year-old girl in Shanghai, whom Jane Qiu calls Mei, was diagnosed with a rare genetic mutation linked to developmental delay and autism-like traits. Her condition was mild. She was improving with therapy and special education. Her parents still paid $860,000 to a team led by Qiu Zilong, a neuroscientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, to develop a gene therapy made for her alone. It used adeno-associated viruses to carry gene editors into the brain, and Xinhua Hospital approved it.

On March 24th 2025 the viral particles were injected into Mei's spinal cord. She developed a fever and kidney failure, and died within days. A year later the team published its preclinical findings in Nature. Chinese media hailed a “world-class breakthrough” without mentioning the dead child or her family's money.

Jane Qiu, a Beijing science writer who has covered Chinese research ethics for two decades, stresses that deaths in early trials are not unusual. What shocks her is the trail of lapses. A Science investigation in July, later confirmed by an inquiry from Shanghai's municipal government, found that the consent form did not mention the possibility of death; that the hospital approved the treatment before toxicology data showed liver and kidney damage in monkeys given similar therapies; and that the researchers did not disclose the death. Her essay in Noema asks what kind of system produces such an outcome.
## Not one bad actor

Qiu's first point is that Mei's case is not isolated. Several researchers told her that Chinese hospitals routinely fail to report adverse events. In August STAT reported a second death, in a gene-editing trial run by HuidaGene, also of Shanghai, which had gone undisclosed for about 15 months; the company published its results, including the fatal case, in Cell on October 26th. The founder of a rare-disease group, speaking anonymously for fear of political repercussions, said she knew of other genetic-disorder trials where deaths went unreported. American lawmakers on the House Select Committee on China have since warned against relying on Chinese trial data.

The pattern, Qiu writes, is familiar. Since modern bioethics reached China in the late 1980s, hype-driven scandals have recurred: foreigners flying in for unproven stem-cell therapies in 2006; bogus online advertising for immunotherapies, curbed only after the death of a 21-year-old student, Wei Zexi; then He Jiankui's announcement of the first gene-edited babies. Each earned China a reputation as biotechnology's “Wild East”. Qiu Zilong, she notes, condemned He's conduct, then faced a comparable scandal six years later.
## The fast track

Beijing did respond to the CRISPR-babies affair. Ethics provisions went into the first Civil Code, a national ethics committee was created and review guidelines were rewritten, under what was reported as Xi Jinping's “ethics first” line. But another policy pulled the opposite way. Healthy China 2030, launched in 2016, prized the rapid clinical use of new technologies, and reforms created a dual track: the conventional route through the National Medical Products Administration, and a technology route overseen by the health ministry.

On the second track sit investigator-initiated trials, or IITs, typically run by university scientists with hospital clinicians. Such trials exist everywhere. What was distinctive in China was that, until new rules took effect in May 2026, they needed only a hospital's approval, with no national review. That made them fast and cheap, and attracted investors. By one estimate more than 40,000 IITs had been registered by April 2026, involving hundreds of thousands of people. Kiran Musunuru of the University of Pennsylvania, who led the personalised gene-editing treatment of the American infant known as Baby KJ, told Qiu that there is a “widespread perception” abroad that China offers quick, cheap first-in-human trials; some American researchers want to copy elements of the model.

The costs show up in quality. Pressure for high-impact papers and hospital rankings pushed researchers into human trials early. Committees sometimes reviewed two dozen proposals in an afternoon, which Zhu Wei, a bioethicist at the Shanghai Clinical Research Center, calls “a rubber-stamping exercise”. One analysis of Chinese stem-cell IITs found that only a small fraction sped up translation; most were repetitive and wasteful. Musunuru argues that few local researchers have the experience to judge the risks of frontier therapies, so approval comes down to their “appetite for risk”. Jing-Bao Nie of the University of Otago points to institutional conflicts of interest, from promotion to prestige, and suggests the lure of a breakthrough may have overwhelmed caution in Mei's case. Politics adds pressure, since senior hospital leaders often chair the review committees.
## Rules without inspectors

State Council Order No. 818, in force since May, tightens things considerably. Only top-tier hospitals may run IITs; gene and cell therapies, brain-machine interfaces, transplants and microbial therapies need further ministry review; adverse events must be reported within five working days; and violations can bring fines, bans, loss of licences and criminal charges. Zhai Xiaomei of Peking Union Medical College, a member of the national ethics committee, says matters have improved, and Qiu agrees.

Yet she sees large gaps. A researcher working with the ministry told her it lacks staff with technical expertise and leans on a handful of outside experts per case, whereas at America's Food and Drug Administration dozens of in-house reviewers may examine one submission. More seriously, the order creates no inspection process and no whistleblowing channel for adverse events, both central to oversight in America and Britain. In a country without a free press, Qiu argues, penalties without detection risk becoming empty threats. Ma Yonghui of Xiamen University worries that military hospitals sit outside ministry rules and that free-trade zones such as Bo'ao on Hainan may get special treatment. Qiu recalls that in October 2018, a month before the gene-edited babies were announced, He Jiankui and the American fertility doctor John Zhang met Hainan's vice-governor to discuss a Bo'ao clinic offering experimental procedures, including heritable genome editing.
## Hope as a market

The final strand of the argument is social. Rare-disease groups have flourished in China, giving families agency in a drug market that has failed such patients worldwide. But desperation creates demand. Qiu describes a three-year-old in Kunming with Menkes syndrome who in 2022 received a gene therapy from a young company with no track record in neurodevelopmental disease, in a trial that appears to have lacked proper efficacy measures; the press reported improvements and played down risks. China has at least 20 million people with rare diseases, and stigma around disability pushes families towards technological fixes for social problems.

Whether Qiu Zilong fed such hopes is unclear; he was fired last week and barred from research for five years, and has not given his account. His book, The Autism Enlightenment, recalls telling the mother of a child with Rett syndrome in 2010 that a cure would probably come in three to five years. It does not mention Jesse Gelsinger, whose death in an American gene-therapy trial in 1999 forced a reckoning, nor the 2024 death in the first brain-directed gene-therapy trial for Rett syndrome. Both used the same kind of viral vector as Mei's treatment.

Qiu hopes Mei's death becomes China's “Gelsinger moment”. That requires regulatory, scientific and social reform at once, and it requires the rest of the world to look past China's few celebrated successes to what she calls a “hidden ocean” of low-quality and potentially harmful trials.
stories.counterpoint: Much of the case rests on anonymous sources, and Qiu cannot quantify how much of China's trial landscape is poor or dangerous. Fast, cheap early trials have also produced genuine advances, and a regime built on fear of the next scandal could slow therapies that families with no other options want. Gelsinger's death did not end hype in America either.
stories.why: China is becoming a major source of first-in-human data for biotech companies everywhere, and Western researchers are openly admiring its speed. If the oversight behind that speed is hollow, the risk is borne by vulnerable children first and by the credibility of global medical evidence second.
questions: When a family pays for an experimental treatment for its own child, who should have the final say over whether it goes ahead?
Is it possible to keep the speed of China's investigator-initiated trials without the lapses Qiu describes, or are they two sides of the same design?
How far should Western regulators and companies trust trial data produced under a system with no inspections or whistleblowing channel?

source.title: What China's Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry
source.author: Jane Qiu

stories.headline: AI's new philanthropists and the questions they fund
stories.dek: Grace Werner argues that AI fortunes will soon pay for most research into AI's consequences, and that the Gilded Age shows why that should worry democrats even when the donors are sincere.
body: Artificial intelligence is producing fortunes on a Gilded Age scale, and the firms that build it already produce most of what is known about it. Citing Stanford's 2026 AI Index, Grace Werner of the Foundation for American Innovation notes that more than 90% of notable AI models now come from private industry. In America and Britain government bodies test frontier models before release, but only under voluntary agreements that developers can decline to renew.

Now the same firms and founders are becoming leading funders of research into AI's consequences. The OpenAI Foundation, which emerged from the company's 2025 restructuring holding roughly a quarter of it, has committed $25 billion to curing diseases and “AI resilience”. Anthropic's IPO filing, made public in October, confirmed that each of its seven cofounders has pledged 80% of personal equity to philanthropy, an amount estimated at nearly $80 billion; the company has also put 5% of its shares into a public-benefit fund and pledged $200 million for outside research on AI's economic effects. The head of Coefficient Giving, formerly Open Philanthropy, reckons AI wealth could add about $40 billion a year to American giving if both labs go public.

Werner, writing in Palladium, does not doubt the donors' sincerity. Her question is structural: if a small Bay Area circle decides which questions attract money and talent, which questions will go unasked, and what institutions can check that power?
## Ludlow and the Rockefeller Plan

Her first precedent is the Rockefeller Foundation. In May 1913 John D. Rockefeller, then the world's richest man, gave $100 million, about a ninth of his fortune, to promote “the well-being of mankind”, under the banner of “scientific philanthropy”. That September more than 10,000 coal miners in southern Colorado struck for better conditions and freedom from company control of their housing and shops. On April 20th 1914 the National Guard and company guards attacked their tent colony at Ludlow and set it alight; about twenty people died, including two women and eleven children. The largest operator in the coalfield was Colorado Fuel and Iron, a Rockefeller company.

Two months later the foundation set up a Department of Industrial Research under William Lyon Mackenzie King, who was also personally advising John D. Rockefeller Jr on the strike. King's work produced the “Rockefeller Plan”, adopted at the company in 1915, which gave miners a company-sponsored grievance channel rather than the independent union they had struck for. It became a template for company unions. Frank Walsh, chairman of Congress's Commission on Industrial Relations, made the foundation itself an object of inquiry, arguing that industry-funded research could entrench an industry's power by shaping what the public believed. Werner thinks the critique applies again, and that the largest bias may lie in what goes unfunded: “the dog that didn't bark”.
## The gospel and its limits

Werner gives the Gilded Age its due. Carnegie's libraries, the University of Chicago and the Rockefeller Institute expanded American intellectual life, and Andrew Carnegie's 1889 essay on wealth, with its claim that the man who dies rich “dies disgraced”, was a better creed than conspicuous consumption. But it assumed that ruthlessness in business would turn easily into wisdom in giving. Donors need not dictate conclusions; they shape a field through what they fund and on what terms.

Her example is Joseph Wharton of Bethlehem Steel, who in 1881 gave $100,000 to the University of Pennsylvania for what became the first collegiate business school. Its early output included Simon Patten's 1890 case for protecting domestic industry, congenial to a steel man, and the school also fostered the field of industrial relations. It declined, however, to renew the professorship of Scott Nearing, an opponent of child labour.
## Capture versus dependence

Werner thinks Dario Amodei's argument that those enriched by AI bear responsibility for its consequences echoes Carnegie, and has real merit. Much of the money will fund work on AI's effects on workers, children, security and the economy, and some theories will suit the labs better than others. AI also raises the stakes. Rockefeller's power was over energy; the AI magnate's is over information, as people delegate thinking to systems the labs control, and even apparently independent organisations may lean on those systems to produce their views.

She draws on Michael Polanyi's “republic of science”: discovery depends on investigators being free to chase unexpected questions, and formal freedom to publish is not the same as the practical means to pursue an unfunded line of inquiry. Problems also have to be described before they can be solved, and policymakers mostly act on problems that are already measured, modelled and packaged as proposals. Governance matters too. Anthropic's filing describes the founders' pledges as voluntary and revocable, and the cofounders keep majority voting control; the OpenAI Foundation is a public charity, free of the holding cap and 5% annual payout that bind private foundations.

Her key distinction is between capture, where an institution serves a private interest instead of the public, and dependence, where honest researchers work within agendas set by a few funders. Ethics rules address the first, not the second. Public money is not neutral either, and private philanthropy can sustain a diversity of inquiry no totalitarian state could. What matters is whether a system supports competing lines of inquiry, so that biased government and biased industry check each other.
## The hollowed-out state

Here Werner turns to the Progressive Era's answer. Tocqueville had praised democracies in which free associations of equal citizens undertook great works, and warned that industry could breed a new aristocracy of manufacturers. Progressive governments built lasting capacity to understand the economy for themselves: the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Federal Trade Commission, agricultural experiment stations and state labour bureaus. Walsh's commission could compel testimony from workers, managers and the richest men in America, producing a record no privately funded body would have made.

That capacity has eroded. Between 1979 and 2015, Werner reports, staff at the Government Accountability Office fell by 44%, at the Congressional Research Service by 28% and on congressional committees by 38%. In 1995 Congress abolished its Office of Technology Assessment. The political scientists Timothy LaPira and Herschel Thomas found that more than half of registered federal lobbyists are former officials, filling what LaPira calls “a vacuum” of expertise in Congress. Dependence deepens itself: the more expertise lives outside government, the easier it is to stop paying for it inside, and the more outsiders can outbid the state for scarce specialists.

Werner's conclusion is sober. Dependence cannot be eliminated, only examined and perhaps mitigated. Progressive reformers acted late, after massacres and unrest, and never solved the problem of epistemic independence. Walsh could make a Rockefeller testify, but he could not decide which questions experts would pursue. That power belonged to whoever paid for the research, and, she writes, it still does.
stories.counterpoint: The analogy may flatter the past and slander the present: AI donors are funding outside researchers, publishing their pledges and inviting scrutiny in ways Rockefeller never did, and much safety research exists only because labs paid for it. Rebuilding state capacity is also no guarantee of independence, since public agencies have their own political masters and blind spots.
stories.why: Within a few years the evidence that shapes laws on AI, from labour-market studies to safety evaluations, may be paid for largely by the companies being regulated. Werner's distinction between capture and dependence gives legislators and readers a sharper test than asking whether donors mean well.
questions: Which questions about AI do you suspect will attract little funding precisely because no one with money benefits from the answer?
Is a researcher who works honestly within a funder's agenda meaningfully less independent than one funded by government?
What would it take for your own country's legislature to have independent expertise on AI, and who would pay for it?

source.title: Who Pays for What We Know
source.author: Grace Werner

stories.headline: The myth of the lucky laboratory accident
stories.dek: Saloni Dattani argues that the most famous tales of accidental discovery are mostly untrue, and that the real stories of rivalry, secrecy and graft are both more interesting and more useful.
body: Everyone loves an accidental discovery. A mould drifts through an open window and gives the world penicillin. A forgotten flask of stale broth yields a vaccine. A glowing screen in a darkened lab reveals X-rays. The stories are charming, easy to retell and flattering to the rest of us, since they suggest that genius is mostly a matter of being in the right room on the right afternoon.

Saloni Dattani, an editor at Works in Progress, thinks they are largely untrue. In a short, sharply argued essay she takes apart three of the best-loved tales, those of Alexander Fleming, Louis Pasteur and Wilhelm Röntgen, and argues that calling such discoveries accidents misleads people about how science actually advances. The truth, she contends, involves deliberate experiment, competition and concealment, and it is a better story than the myth.

Her subtitle, “let the facts spoil a good dinner party story”, sets the tone. This is not a debunking for its own sake. Her point is that if we misunderstand how discoveries were made, we will be worse at making more of them.
## The window that never opened

The popular version of penicillin's discovery has spores floating in through an open window and dissolving a plate of bacteria. Dattani finds three problems. First, Fleming's own 1929 paper says nothing about where the spores came from, though she concedes that, being microscopic, he may simply not have known. Second, he first told the window story in a 1945 interview, sixteen years later, and colleagues said the window was seldom if ever opened. Third, and most damning, nobody could reproduce the result as he described it. Penicillin interferes with the formation of bacterial cell walls, so it must be present before bacteria grow; it does not dissolve established colonies.

The most convincing reconstruction came from Ronald Hare, who set out to write Fleming's biography and made dozens of attempts to recreate the plate. He found one sequence that fitted the evidence. The spores were an unusually productive strain from a fungal researcher's laboratory on the floor below. They landed on the plate at about the time Fleming seeded it with bacteria. Fleming then forgot to incubate it, and a spell of cold weather let the mould grow before the bacteria could. Hare thought the odds of all this “almost astronomical”, yet came to believe it. Dattani read his notes and letters at the Wellcome Library and agrees with him, because he checked each step against several witnesses and sources.

So there was luck in Fleming's story, but not the luck of legend. It was a chain of coincidences, a neighbour's mould, a forgotten incubator and a cold snap, rather than a single breeze through a window.
## The assistant and the wedding

Pasteur's chicken-cholera vaccine is usually told as a tale of neglect: a broth left exposed to oxygen goes stale, Pasteur uses it anyway when fresh supplies run out, and the chickens turn out to be protected. Historians who have worked through his papers tell a different story. The key experiments were deliberate, and they were carried out by his assistant, Émile Roux, while Pasteur was away at his daughter's wedding.

We know this only because Pasteur's secrecy failed after his death. He forbade his family from publishing his notes and letters; his grandson released them anyway, and historians used them to reconstruct the work. Roux, for his part, had his own notes burned periodically.
## Burned notebooks

Röntgen's story, of a fluorescent screen glowing beside a cathode-ray tube wrapped in cardboard, may be true. But Röntgen had his notes burned after his death, so Dattani treats it as a hypothesis that cannot be checked. She also recounts his long dispute with Philipp Lenard, who had spent years studying cathode rays, had shared his methods and his discharge tube with Röntgen, and later accused him of stealing the discovery. Historians have suggested that this quarrel may explain the bonfire, though without the notes nobody can be sure.

Dattani is careful not to overreach. Some accidents are real. Colchicine was used for centuries against gout before it was found to help in cardiovascular disease, and sildenafil was being tested for angina when its more famous effect was noticed. Side effects are hard to predict, so such finds are plausible. Her target is the tidy myth, not the role of chance altogether.
## The prepared mind

Why do the myths survive? Partly, she argues, because they are better stories. The real explanations involve several coincidences, and readers forget the middle of a convoluted chain. The myths also make scientists seem like ordinary people who got lucky, which is reassuring.

Pasteur's own maxim, that chance favours only the prepared mind, contains some truth. The skill of these scientists lay less in the first observation than in seeing its potential and developing it. Edward Jenner was not the first to notice that cowpox seemed to protect against smallpox, but he documented the effect thoroughly, popularised the method and helped spread vaccination around the world. In Pasteur's case, Dattani argues, the accident framing is almost the opposite of the truth: he and Roux ran hundreds of experiments to find reliable ways of making new vaccines, and calling the result luck erases that work.

She cites her colleague Niko McCarty, who has examined other supposedly serendipitous breakthroughs in biology, including green fluorescent protein and nanopore sequencing, and concluded that they came from systematic trial and error. McCarty also describes “engineered serendipity”. The inventors of optogenetics wrote down exactly what their tool would need to do, then listed every way they could imagine meeting those requirements. Understanding how discoveries really happen, Dattani suggests, might help researchers produce them on purpose.
## Why scientists hide their work

The last question is why credit so often goes to chance, and why scientists hide or burn their notebooks. Embarrassment at mess and mistakes and a wish for privacy may play a part, but Dattani favours competition. The historian Gerald Geison suggested that Pasteur's method for weakening chicken-cholera cultures was “remarkably simple”, and that revealing it early would have invited rivals. Pasteur was probably the best-paid scientist in France and sold his inventions commercially, and because medicines could not then be patented in France, secrecy was the way to protect a monopoly. He did not let collaborators take notes, carried his notebooks when he travelled, and published methods, thinly, only months after announcing results.

Her conclusion is that science, designed to guard against bias, is still run by people who forget things, hide notebooks, burn papers and fight over credit. It is shaped by incentives, rivalries, obsessions and years of unglamorous work. That, she writes, is far more interesting than an open window.
stories.counterpoint: Dattani's case on Fleming rests heavily on one biographer's reconstruction, and on Röntgen she admits the evidence was burned, so her verdicts are probabilistic too. A critic might add that her own account still contains a great deal of luck, from a neighbour's unusual mould to a cold snap, which arguably vindicates the importance of serendipity rather than refuting it.
stories.why: How a society tells the story of discovery shapes how it funds and organises research. If breakthroughs are lucky accidents, there is little to plan; if they come from systematic search, competition and incentives, institutions can be designed to produce more of them.
questions: Which story of discovery in your own field do you repeat without ever having checked it?
If secrecy once protected inventors who could not patent medicines, what incentives today push researchers to hide their methods?
Where in your work could you practise engineered serendipity, writing down exactly what you need and listing every way to get it?

source.title: Science isn't a series of lucky accidents
source.author: Saloni Dattani

stories.headline: Cracks appear in the standard model of the cosmos
stories.dek: Charlie Wood reports that the final results of the 20-year Dark Energy Survey, combined with other data, suggest cosmology's leading model is missing something, though no one yet knows what.
body: In the 1990s Joshua Frieman was one of a handful of physicists who suspected the universe needed some additional “missing energy”. When he and a colleague organised a workshop on the idea in 1997, only a few dozen people signed up. Then, early in 1998, two teams reported that distant supernovae appeared to be accelerating away from Earth, pointing to an unknown repulsive force. Suddenly the workshop drew the press.

Within a few years cosmologists had concluded that this dark energy makes up roughly two-thirds of the universe, with ordinary and dark matter accounting for the rest. Frieman went on to co-found the Dark Energy Survey (DES), a two-decade effort to study it through its effects on the visible universe. In May 2026 DES released findings from its full dataset of thousands of supernovae and hundreds of millions of galaxies. Writing in Quanta, Charlie Wood reports that, combined with other observations, the results show what Simone Ferraro of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory calls “cracks” in the standard model of cosmology.
## Reconstructing a life story

Wood likens experimental cosmology to rebuilding a person's life from scattered records, school reports here and medical tests there. Scientists build a story from the data, gather more, and revise. Earlier generations had already concluded that galaxies need large amounts of invisible dark matter to explain their rotation, and assumed that cosmic expansion was slowing under the pull of all that matter. Puzzles such as stars that seemed older than the universe pushed theorists to add a new kind of energy. The 1998 supernova results then showed that expansion was speeding up, and by the end of that year the cause had a name.

The data at the time were thin: a blurry image of the cosmic microwave background, several million galaxies and a few dozen supernovae. Because light takes time to travel, each observation is a snapshot of an earlier era, so the record covered only part of cosmic history.
## Twenty years of looking

DES began in 2003 with physicists at Fermilab. The team built the Dark Energy Camera, a 570-megapixel instrument that Wood describes as the most powerful digital camera of its era, and mounted it on the four-metre Victor M. Blanco Telescope in the Chilean Andes. It observed for 758 nights between 2013 and 2019, a year longer than planned to make up for cloudy weather during a strong El Niño. The collaboration grew to more than 400 scientists in seven countries.

For years its interim results fitted the reigning model, Lambda-CDM, in which the universe is about 30% matter, mostly cold dark matter, and about 70% dark energy. In that model dark energy is “lambda”, a constant property of empty space, so expansion accelerates steadily as space grows.

The first serious challenge came from elsewhere. The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), at Kitt Peak in Arizona, uses thousands of small robotic positioners, each aimed at a single galaxy. It measures spherical shells of matter left by sound waves in the early universe. Because each shell has a known physical size, its apparent size on the sky reveals its distance, and from those distances researchers can chart how the expansion rate has changed over roughly the past 10 billion of the universe's 13.8 billion years. In 2024 DESI reported that adding these shells to existing data made Lambda-CDM fit poorly, while a model in which dark energy weakens over time fitted better. A 2025 analysis with more data agreed.
## Measuring the clumping

DES worked on a different chapter of the record: how matter has clumped over time. Gravity pulls matter together while dark energy pushes it apart, so the degree of clumping in each era reveals dark energy's strength. Sujeong Lee of Ohio University explained to Wood that DES measures this in two ways, by how visible galaxies cluster in the centres of dark-matter haloes, and by how dark matter bends light from background galaxies. Both require comparing hundreds of millions of galaxies for subtle distortions in position and shape.

After seven years of analysis DES published its final results early in 2026. Ferraro, who is not a member, called the work “a real tour de force”. The team also reprocessed a catalogue of 1,600 supernovae; Seshadri Nadathur, a DESI cosmologist, said he trusted the reanalysed data more than any other supernova set, and Wood notes that the leading catalogues now agree closely.

When DES combined its clumping maps, its supernovae, DESI's shells and microwave-background data, Lambda-CDM struggled. The survey reported a three-sigma preference for weakening dark energy. That is enough to command attention but well short of the five-sigma threshold physicists demand before claiming a discovery. What makes the result harder to dismiss, Wood explains, is that the mismatch does not come from one rogue dataset. Under Lambda-CDM the microwave background disagrees with the matter maps, the matter maps disagree with the supernovae, and the supernovae disagree with the microwave background. No single dataset can be dropped to restore harmony, which makes a statistical fluke from stitching many observations together less likely. As Ferraro puts it, “there's something that doesn't fit.”
## Mystery upon mystery

What doesn't fit is contested. Some theorists doubt that dark energy really changes. Explaining why the energy of the vacuum is as small as it is was already a major unsolved problem; explaining why that tiny energy is also slowly decaying would compound the problem.

Others suspect a different assumption is wrong. One candidate is the timing of reionisation, when the first stars and other bright objects burned away the hydrogen fog of the early universe. Lambda-CDM puts it about 700 million years after the Big Bang. In a 2025 analysis Ferraro and colleagues found that if it happened about 200 million years earlier, the standard model would fit the data better. The number is crucial, Ferraro says, but extremely hard to measure. Still other theorists are exploring forms of dark energy that change in step with the mass of dark matter.

Answers will come from more data. DESI will keep observing until at least 2028, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory on Cerro Pachón, about six miles from DES's old home on Cerro Tololo, began survey operations in 2026. With the world's largest digital camera it is expected to catalogue some 10 billion galaxies and millions of supernovae, and former DES researchers are joining it. Dark energy was discovered with a few dozen supernovae. Wood ends by noting that cosmology, after two stable decades, is once again a field with open questions.
stories.counterpoint: Three-sigma anomalies in physics have a long history of evaporating as systematics are understood, and the combined result depends on stitching together very different instruments, each with its own calibration choices. A sceptic would say the honest headline is not that dark energy is weakening but that cosmologists' error bars may be too small.
stories.why: Lambda-CDM underpins almost every estimate of the universe's age, contents and fate. If dark energy is not a constant, physics faces a new problem at the boundary of gravity and quantum theory, and the next few years of data from DESI and Rubin will decide whether this is a revolution or a correction.
questions: How much weight should a three-sigma result carry when it comes from several independent datasets all pointing the same way?
Is it more plausible that dark energy changes, or that a hard-to-measure assumption such as the timing of reionisation is wrong?
What does it mean for a science to return to open questions after two decades of a model that seemed to work?

source.title: What Makes Up the Cosmos? A 20-Year Survey Hints That Something Is Missing.
source.author: Charlie Wood

stories.headline: Horses, not harvests, built the first states
stories.dek: Lhamsuren Munkh-Erdene argues that states arose from animal and boat transport and the conquests it allowed, and that the grain-centred story owes much to Cold War politics.
body: Most popular histories of civilisation begin in a field of wheat. Farming produced surpluses, surpluses fed cities and officials, and officials built states. Writers from Jared Diamond to James C. Scott have told versions of this story, Scott in a sceptical key: grain, being easy to see, measure and tax, made peasants governable.

Lhamsuren Munkh-Erdene, a historian and anthropologist at the National University of Mongolia, thinks the story starts in the wrong place. In a long essay for Aeon he argues that the foundation of the state was not grain but transport, above all domesticated animals and boats, and the conquest that mobility made possible. The first states, on this account, were made by warbands that could move, and often by pastoral nomads who never farmed at all.
He opens with a modern reminder of how much power still depends on movement: the Strait of Hormuz, and the oil that, he says, fuels more than 90% of global transport.
## The limit of the walking community

His starting point is a physical constraint. Before animal or boat transport, communities could produce only what people could carry on foot. Settlements stayed small and dispersed, like those of the Amazon basin or the New Guinea highlands, and their size kept them relatively undifferentiated and egalitarian, a kind of natural immunity to inequality. Domesticated animals and boats broke that ceiling, allowing larger communities to form and armed groups to project force across large territories.

The historical roll-call is long. At sea, Vikings had longships, the Aztecs canoes, the Egyptians riverboats, and Romans, Greeks and Phoenicians their galleys. On land, equids made states and llamas served the Inka. He points to the war-wagons drawn by kunga, a donkey hybrid, at Ur as evidence of Mesopotamian military power, to the donkeys buried at Abydos alongside early Egyptian kingship, to the Sintashta nomads who buried chariots with their rulers around 2000 BC, and to the 4,000 chariots with which the Zhou are said to have defeated the Shang in 1046 BC. Pizarro conquered the Inka with horses; the Comanche, with horses, contested European powers for nearly a century.

The Comanche matter to the argument because they had no agriculture. They lived by horse husbandry and bison hunting, yet built an empire. The great steppe powers, the Mongols included, were likewise pastoralists with abundant animals and little farm produce. Each empire, Rome or Mongol, could go wherever its transport could go. Building a state, he concludes, requires extrahuman transport, not grain.
## How a paradigm was made

Why, then, does the grain story dominate? Munkh-Erdene's most provocative claim is that it rests on what he calls a Sinocentric paradigm, which places China and its agrarian civilisation at the centre of world history and treats steppe empires as marginal or anomalous. He traces it to Owen Lattimore's Inner Asian Frontiers of China (1940), on which Scott drew.

Lattimore, he argues, had earlier accepted that nomadic conquerors founded many Chinese states, but recast Inner Asia as a frontier, stateless and barbarian, in ways that served the Republic of China's claims over Mongolia, Manchuria, Tibet and Eastern Turkestan as those regions broke away between 1911 and 1933. By the author's account, recognising the Qing, which he calls the Daiching, as an Inner Asian empire would have cost China about two-thirds of its claimed territory, on Lattimore's own estimate. Lattimore, he says, reframed mobility as an anti-state, dispersing force and grain as the source of wealth and power; used “dynastic cycles” to turn conquests into mere changes of ruling house; and described an “absorptive” Chinese empire that assimilated its conquerors.

The paradigm was then globalised. Robert Carneiro's 1970 “circumscription” theory held that hemmed-in farmland produced population pressure and thus states, and was popularised by Michael Mann, Jared Diamond, Francis Fukuyama and Yuval Noah Harari. Yet settlement surveys in Mesopotamia, the Nile valley and coastal Peru found no overcrowding, and some regions depopulated while states were forming. Scott's response, adding drought as a kind of climatic circumscription that turns Uruk's roughly 250 hectares into a farming enclave, strikes the author as a clever way to save the paradigm rather than test it.
## The archaeology of the steppe

Munkh-Erdene also challenges the assumption that herding grew out of farming. Melinda Zeder's work suggests plants and animals were domesticated at about the same time, around 11,500 years ago if not earlier, often in different regions, with pastoralists domesticating equids along their own path. He cites evidence of horse-riding nomadism and animal art around 1500 BC near the Black Sea, spreading east to the Ordos. He faults the neo-evolutionary ladders of Elman Service and Morton Fried, band to tribe to chiefdom to state, for making intensive agriculture the precondition of statehood.

He turns the numbers on China itself. Inner Asian nomads, he argues, ruled agricultural populations from the rise of the Shang to the fall of the Qing in 1912. Victor Mair counted 83 polities in the region and found only 31 were Sinitic, with the Qin and Han likely carrying a Central Eurasian heritage; Hugh Clark estimated that outsiders ruled the North China Plain for about two of the last three millennia. Even the romantic view of mobility as freedom, found in Scott and in David Graeber and David Wengrow's The Dawn of Everything, strikes him as the grain thesis in another guise.
## Conquest and charisma

In place of the grain story he offers conquest theory, built on Max Weber. If the state is a community claiming a monopoly of legitimate force within a territory, then its origin lies in the warband, its monopoly in the warlord and its birthplace in a state of war, which makes violence legitimate by making security paramount. Transport enabled mobilisation; nomads conquered farmers; bureaucracy followed sovereignty rather than creating it. He accuses Service and Fried of distorting Weber's idea of charisma, “the great revolutionary force”, and of equating the state with bureaucracy, and he rejects Fukuyama's claim that China alone created a modern state.

He insists this does not glorify conquest, which he says produced despotic, two-tier class states. He also argues that charismatic revolutions drive progress, even if they later harden into institutional traps. His aim is a history that restores human agency, charisma and the Eurasian steppe to the centre. The grain paradigm, he concludes, makes the mistake of attributing cultural outcomes to nature and natural limits to culture.
stories.counterpoint: The essay attributes political motives to Lattimore and intellectual evasions to Scott and others that it asserts more than demonstrates, and several of its numbers, such as the Zhou chariot count, rest on traditional sources. Grain and transport are also not exclusive: most conquest states depended on taxing settled farmers, so a critic might say the author has found a second necessary condition rather than overturned the first.
stories.why: Theories of where states come from shape how people think about inequality, freedom and the legitimacy of power today. If states began with mobile warbands rather than granaries, then logistics, transport and coercion deserve more attention than surplus and bureaucracy in explaining how political order is made and unmade.
questions: Does it matter whether the first states were built on grain or on transport, if both ended up taxing farmers?
How far should a scholar's political context, such as Lattimore's, change how much we trust his conclusions?
Where do you see control of movement, of goods, people or information, functioning as the real foundation of power today?

recall.headline: Whose wanting are you working for?
recall.dek: Luke Burgis's account of borrowed desire suggests that the most important question about a goal is not whether it is good, but where it came from.
body: Think of the last thing you wanted badly enough to rearrange your week for it. A promotion, a particular car, a course, a number on a dashboard. Now try to remember the first time you wanted it. Very often there is a person standing at that moment: a colleague who got there first, a friend who mentioned it casually, a stranger on a screen who seemed to have it and seemed untroubled. The want arrived feeling like yours. It may have been on loan.

That is the central claim of Luke Burgis's book Wanting, which popularises the French thinker René Girard's theory of mimetic desire. Once our basic needs are met, Burgis argues, we enter a different world, the world of desire, and knowing what to want is much harder than knowing what we need. We solve the problem the way children do. We watch other people and want what they want.
## Models, not preferences

Burgis calls the people who show us what is worth wanting models. They are not the same as role models in the motivational sense. A model can be a rival, an acquaintance or a brand. What matters is that their wanting makes an object seem desirable. He notes that infants begin imitating within seconds of birth, and that pre-verbal babies track what other people desire before they have words for it. Imitation is not a flaw we acquire; it is how we are built.

The danger, in his account, lies in what he calls the romantic lie: the story we tell ourselves that we chose something because of its objective qualities, or because it suited our unique tastes. Models are most powerful when hidden. If you want someone to be passionate about a thing, Burgis observes, they must believe the passion is their own.

Two further points from the book are worth keeping. First, rivalry is a function of proximity. We do not compete with celebrities, because they are too distant to take our desires seriously. We compete with the colleague two desks away, the former classmate, the founder who launched the same month. Second, the more two rivals fight, the more alike they become. Burgis tells of a friend at a start-up who began staying later each night simply because a talented colleague did, until both were pulling all-nighters the work did not require. When the colleague left to found a company, the friend founded one three months later, and bought Bitcoin when the rival did. Only after he deliberately stopped following the other man's news, starving the rivalry of oxygen, did he describe himself as free of it.
## Thin and thick desires

Burgis does not conclude that we should stop imitating. That would be impossible and, he argues, undesirable: imitation and innovation belong to the same process, and some of the most creative people begin by copying the right model. The aim is discernment, telling apart the desires worth keeping from those that will leave us empty.

His distinction here is between thin and thick desires. Thin desires are intense, fast and borrowed. They flare up through contagion and fade once the object is reached, like the retirement someone longs for over decades and finds hollow on arrival. Thick desires are quieter and grow over time. Wanting to spend more time with one's family is his example: it can be started today and keeps paying out, compounding over years. He adds an observation that rings true: the feelings attached to a desire are often more intense the thinner it is.
## A practical test

What follows is my own synthesis, not a procedure Burgis lays out in these terms. It combines three of his suggestions, naming your models, separating judgments from the crowd and ranking values, into a single check you can run on any goal.

Take one goal you are pursuing this quarter and ask three questions of it. Who first showed me this was worth wanting? If you can name a person, ask whether you admire their life or merely their position relative to yours. Would I still want this if no one could see me get it? A goal that survives invisibility is more likely to be thick. And if I imagine the end of my working life, does this desire still look like something I would be glad to have served? Burgis suggests that the deathbed is where thin desires are exposed, and that it is better to visit it in imagination now.

Consider a practical case. A manager notices she has been eyeing a larger team. Running the test, she realises the want arrived the week a peer was promoted to lead one. She does not admire that peer's working life, which is long hours and constant meetings. Asked whether she would want the role if no one knew she had it, she hesitates. What she does want, when she looks harder, is the chance to develop two junior colleagues properly, which needs no promotion at all and can begin on Monday. The goal changes from a rung on a ladder to a practice she can start. Nothing about the larger team was wrong in itself. It simply turned out to be someone else's want, worn for a few weeks as her own. The development work, by contrast, passes all three questions, and is the kind of desire that should grow thicker with use rather than fade once reached.

Burgis offers a related discipline for groups. When people vote or judge in public, he notes, they copy one another, so independent judgment needs independent conditions: ballots that cannot be seen, opinions written down before discussion. The same applies within a single head. Write down what you want before you scroll, before the meeting, before you hear what your rival did.
## Why it matters

None of this makes desire suspect in itself. Imitation is how we learn to love good things as well as trivial ones. The point is to see the mechanism, because a borrowed want that goes unexamined can steer years of effort. Burgis's deepest warning is that we assume we are the exception, immune to the crowd. The habit worth building is the modest one of asking, regularly, where a want came from, and keeping the ones that grow thicker the longer we hold them.
questions: Name one goal you are chasing this month: who first modelled it for you, and would you still want it if no one could see you reach it?
sources: Luke Burgis, Wanting: The Power of Mimetic Desire in Everyday Life (drawing on René Girard's mimetic theory).
